title: Research apprenticeship and qualifying exams
stage: Graduate study and qualifying exams in mathematics
audience: a graduate student in the first years of a mathematics PhD preparing for qualifying exams, or a graduate preparing to apply for one
purpose: Complete the first milestones of a research career in mathematics: prepare systematically for written and oral qualifying exams in analysis, algebra and topology, read research papers and surveys, choose an advisor and a problem, write and typeset an expository paper on a recent topic, present it, and learn how mathematical research, publishing and careers work.
primary_reading: arXiv, the open archive of mathematics preprints

weeks.1: How qualifying exams work and how to prepare
weeks.2: Building a reading list and a study plan
weeks.3: Qualifying exam review: real and complex analysis
weeks.5: Qualifying exam review: topology and geometry
weeks.8: Choosing an advisor and a problem
weeks.12: Paths in mathematics: academia, industry and teaching

blocks.deliverable: Write a twelve-week study plan for your program's qualifying exams.
Take a timed mock exam in analysis and grade it with a rubric.
Take a mock oral exam on a supplied syllabus.
Week 7 midterm; write a one-page summary of a research paper.
Draft an expository paper on a recent topic.
Give a recorded twenty-minute talk on your paper.
Submit the project; take an unseen 180 minute final in week 14.

project: Expository paper and talk: choose a theorem proved in the last fifty years, read the original paper and a survey, write an eight- to twelve-page expository paper in LaTeX that a first-year graduate student could follow, give a recorded twenty-minute talk, and pass a final mock qualifying exam across analysis, algebra and topology.
completion: finish the project, take the week 7 midterm and week 14 cumulative final, then complete a new cumulative assessment after 1 to 2 weeks. Explain one major idea aloud without notes.
